domains.note: No databases, search terms, dates or inclusion criteria are reported; the only stated selection rule is the exclusion of studies with HIV-positive participants (p. 592).

Tables 1–4 give a caveats entry for the tabulated studies (dose, route, sample size, education, other drug use, comparison with norms; pp. 590–604) and the text critiques individual chronic-use studies, but no criteria or tool are stated. The normative comparisons used to appraise McCann et al. (2008) and Simon et al. (2002) give no norms, cut-offs or values (pp. 596, 602).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 7 of the 52 tabulated studies are from the first author's laboratory (Comer 2001; Hart 2001, 2002, 2008; Kirkpatrick 2008, in press; Marrone 2010; reference list p. 606), all among the 16 acute studies of Table 1 (pp. 590–591), and Hart et al. (2002, 2008) are the two acute studies described in detail (pp. 589, 592). The other 9 acute studies are also scored as improvement or no effect, and none of the 36 chronic-use studies in Tables 2–4 is the authors' own.

The critiques of primary studies separate results from their authors' interpretations (pp. 596–602) and the crack-cocaine parallel is labelled speculation (p. 605), but the Conclusions call the cognitive-impairment link 'not supported by evidence from research' and concerns about cognitive-behavioural treatment 'not warranted' (p. 605), the latter with no treatment study reviewed.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against cognitive impairment
domains.note: Under-represented: the evidence for impairment. The one meta-analysis in the reference list (Scott et al., 2007) is cited only as the source of the prevailing view (p. 587), animal evidence of deficits gets one sentence before its dosing regimens are questioned (p. 589), and each user–control difference discussed in the text is followed by reasons to doubt its clinical significance (pp. 596–604).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, because the search and selection are not reported and the review is written against the prevailing view, with the evidence for impairment under-represented. It may be cited for its specific criticisms of individual primary studies (each to be confirmed against the primary paper), for its distinction between a statistically significant group difference and clinical impairment (p. 596), and as a pointer to the acute-dosing studies in Table 1. It may not be cited as evidence that methamphetamine use leaves cognition unimpaired, nor for its comparisons with normative data, which cannot be checked.

sc_hart_2012.where_read: PDF text extraction (Hart_2012_CognitiveFunctioning.txt), PDF pages 1–23 = printed pp. 586–608, read start to end: abstract, all sections, Tables 1–4, acknowledgements, disclosure and reference list.

domains.note: No databases, terms or dates are reported for any of the six hypotheses; inclusion criteria are explicit only for the cross-sectional hypothesis (p. 261), plus a longitudinal-only rule for brain studies (pp. 264–265), so statements such as 'Only two longitudinal studies' (p. 264) cannot be checked for completeness.

Table 1 records matched, statistically controlled and unmatched variables for 15 cross-sectional studies (pp. 262–263), and the text names missing urinalysis, absent retested controls and post hoc testing (pp. 263–267). Animal studies are not appraised, and brain changes with abstinence are called 'convincing' (pp. 265, 269) although the only DAT study with retested controls had 5 users and no statistical group comparison and the grey-matter figure uses an uncorrected threshold (pp. 265–266).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: About 10 of roughly 130 references are from the authors' group (Groman 2012; Simon 2010; Morales 2012 and Berman 2007, 'from the same laboratory'; Monterosso 2005; Dean 2012; others), including the only monkey study (p. 260), two of the three brain studies with retested controls (p. 265), both figures (pp. 266, 268) and the education analysis (pp. 267–268). One of them, Simon et al. (2010), is reported as null (pp. 261, 264).

The conclusion is framed as a judgment on indirect evidence (pp. 260, 268), but Iudicello et al. (2010) is summarized as showing that users impaired at baseline improve (pp. 264, 269) although the text reports a post hoc trend (p=0.06; p. 264), and brain changes during abstinence are called 'highly likely' to reflect direct effects of methamphetamine (p. 269). The abstract's 'possibility' (p. 259) becomes 'does cause' in the Discussion (p. 268).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against methamphetamine-caused cognitive decline
domains.note: Under-represented: evidence that the differences predate use, which gets one sentence on childhood predictors (p. 259) and a sibling study set aside as mostly cocaine (p. 263), although null results are reported under each hypothesis (pp. 261, 263–267) and Hart et al. are answered (p. 270). Bonferroni-corrected null results are discounted as over-conservative (p. 261), and animal studies are weighted most heavily (p. 268) despite the dose-translation caveat (p. 260).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, because no search is reported for any hypothesis and selection is explicit for only one, and several lines of the argument rest on the authors' own studies; within those limits the review reports which hypotheses failed, notably dose–response. It may be cited for the structure of the indirect causal argument, for the absence of dose–response evidence, and for Table 1 and its vote counts as pointers to matched cross-sectional studies. It may not be cited as evidence that methamphetamine causes cognitive decline or that cognition or brain markers recover with abstinence; those claims need the primary studies.

sc_dean_2013.where_read: PDF text extraction (Dean_2013_EvidenceCognitiveDecline.txt), PDF pages 1–16 = printed pp. 259–274, read start to end: abstract, introduction, all six hypothesis sections, moderators, discussion and conclusion, Table 1, Figure 1–2 legends, acknowledgements, disclosure and reference list.

domains.note: A search of PubMed and national survey databases with dates (April and September 2014) and terms is reported (Introduction, last paragraph), but no eligibility criteria, record counts or selection process; the only stated principle is to incorporate the most recent reports and reviews.

The cited studies are not appraised: frequency, duration and recurrence figures are given without design or quality comments (Sections 2–3.3), and the only quality remark on a specific study is that one trial was small (N=58; 5.1). Persistence figures of 16% and 17% from two smaller studies are called 'very similar' to the nearly 40% Thai figure (3.2).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 4 of 99 references are the authors' own (Methamphetamine Treatment Project papers, refs 10, 11 and 96; a chapter co-written by the second author, ref 87); ref 10 is the only source given for engagement and reduced use with Matrix Model treatment among people with psychosis (2.1).

The abstract calls psychosocial treatment of methamphetamine dependence the optimal first-line approach to reducing psychosis, while the body presents this as an argument ('it has been argued', 2.1) and cites no trial with psychosis as the outcome (5.2). The Key points say recommendations 'will involve' neuroleptics regardless of etiology, against the body's statements that evidence is insufficient for guidelines and that most cases may resolve without medication (5.1).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the course and treatment of methamphetamine psychosis
domains.note: Neither side is under-represented: competing explanations for persistent psychosis (a prolonged methamphetamine psychosis, unmasked schizophrenia, a continuum; 3.2) and both the efficacy and the risks of antipsychotics (5.1) are presented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, because the selection of sources is unstated, the cited studies are not appraised, and the abstract and Key points state treatment conclusions that the body presents as argued or unproven. It may be cited for its account of the DSM-5 and ICD-10 criteria and of the diagnostic approach (timeline of use, collateral information, urine toxicology, PRISM), and as a pointer to primary studies. Its frequency, duration and recurrence figures and its treatment recommendations may not be cited without the primary sources.

sc_glasner_edwards_2014.where_read: Saved PubMed Central page text of the NIH author manuscript (PMC5027896; glasner.txt), read start to end: abstract, Sections 1–6, Key points, footnotes (disclosures, funding) and references 1–99; the manuscript has no tables or figures.

domains.note: Three databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, ScienceDirect), reference lists and Google Scholar were searched with printed terms against inclusion criteria set before the search (Overview of review › Inclusion criteria; Search approach). There are no search dates, record counts or excluded-study list, one author conducted the review (Author contributions), and Hajebi et al. (2018), used in the text and Table 2, is missing from Table 1.

Table 2 records for each of 13 studies the comparison groups, acute/chronic distinction, abstinence and factors controlled, and the text names study limitations, but there is no validated tool. Okada, Yamamuro and Srisurapanont are assigned to acute or chronic psychosis differently across Table 1, Table 2 and the text, and the review's main contrasts depend on that assignment.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Neither author appears in any of the 140 references, including the 13 compared studies (References; Tables 1–2).

The abstract concludes that acute methamphetamine psychosis could be clinically distinguished from schizophrenia by thought disorder, hallucination type and parietal-mediated attention, while the body calls the thought-disorder evidence 'indirect and inconclusive' and the hallucination comparisons not 'reliable' (Positive symptoms › Acute, 3rd–4th paragraphs) and the parietal link rests on one attention test without imaging (Cognitive symptoms › Acute, 2nd paragraph). The management paragraph states that acute symptoms will resolve with abstinence, citing a StatPearls chapter (Summary and conclusions, 3rd paragraph).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for similarity and difference between methamphetamine psychosis and schizophrenia
domains.note: Neither side is under-represented: similar and divergent findings are reported study by study, and the introduction sets out competing explanations (shared vulnerability, methamphetamine-caused schizophrenia, a distinct disorder). The limitations section's arguments on power and total-score scales run only toward differences being missed (Methodological limitations, 3rd paragraph).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, because the abstract's central conclusion, that acute methamphetamine psychosis can be told apart from schizophrenia, rests on evidence the body itself calls indirect or inconclusive; the search and the appraisal of studies are reported but incomplete. It may be cited as a map of the 12–13 direct-comparison studies and their shared limitations (small, mostly hospital samples; unreported abstinence; uncontrolled polydrug use and medication) and for the point that few studies separate acute from persistent psychosis. It may not be cited for any symptom that distinguishes the two conditions, nor for its introductory prevalence and duration figures.

sc_wearne_2018.where_read: Saved PubMed Central page text (PMC6191498; wearne.txt), read start to end: abstract, all sections, Tables 1–2 as text, Figure 1 legend (image not available), author contributions, conflict statement, acknowledgments and references 1–140.

domains.note: There is no methods section: no databases, dates or selection criteria are reported, and only the scope (structural, molecular and functional imaging, focused on cortical and striatal abnormalities) is stated (Abstract).

There is no appraisal of the cited studies as such; limitations are named for some findings (smoking and familial explanations for structural data, polydrug use in Boileau et al., 2012, conflicting VMAT2 results; Structural Brain Imaging, 4th–7th paragraphs; Monoamine systems, 3rd and 5th paragraphs). The recovery evidence (two DAT studies of 5 users each; Figure 1 at p<0.005 uncorrected) is presented without comment on size or threshold (Structural Brain Imaging, 3rd paragraph; Monoamine systems, 2nd paragraph).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Six of the 142 bibliography entries name a review author (Ballard 2014, a poster; Kohno 2013, 2014; London 2004; Morales 2012; Payer 2011), and at least six 'et al.' entries are from the senior author's group by the author lists printed in Hart et al. (2012) and Dean et al. (2013) (e.g., Lee 2009, Monterosso 2005, Simon 2010). These supply 3 of the 4 figures, the grey-matter recovery claim, the risky decision-making and resting-state findings, and 3 of the 4 citations for common executive deficits (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).

The abstract presents group differences as corticostriatal 'dysfunction' without the body's caveats that human studies cannot assign structural differences to methamphetamine and that smoking or familial factors may explain some (Structural Brain Imaging, 4th–7th paragraphs). The claim that grey-matter deficits reverse with protracted abstinence rests on one month of abstinence shown at an uncorrected threshold (3rd paragraph; Figure 1), and lower fractional anisotropy is read as drug-induced damage in the 5th paragraph and as familial predisposition in the 7th.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against methamphetamine-caused brain and cognitive deficits
domains.note: Under-represented: evidence that the functional and cognitive differences are small, absent or not caused by methamphetamine; counter-evidence is given for structural findings (Structural Brain Imaging, 4th–7th paragraphs) and a few molecular ones (Monoamine systems, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs) but not for these. Hart et al. (2012) is not in the bibliography, and Simon et al. (2010), listed with no significant differences in Dean et al. (2013, Table 1), is cited only for common executive deficits (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, because there is no search or selection method, the abstract and section-level claims go beyond the evidence and caveats the body itself gives, and a notable share of the evidence comes from the authors' group. It may be cited as a pointer to primary imaging studies marker by marker, and for its own statement that human studies cannot attribute structural differences to methamphetamine. It may not be cited as evidence of methamphetamine-caused deficits, of recovery with abstinence, or of common executive-function deficits.
